facts.claim: Royel Otis's "Linger (SiriusXM Session)" is a cover of The Cranberries' 1992 song "Linger".
Deezer credits the track's writing to Dolores O'Riordan and its composing to Dolores O'Riordan and Noel Hogan. Both are Cranberries members.
The duo recorded the cover for SiriusXM's Alt Nation channel at the SiriusXM studios in New York City. They also performed their own song "Sofa King" in the same session.
The cover came soon after the duo's viral version of Sophie Ellis-Bextor's "Murder on the Dancefloor".
The duo chose "Linger" in a panic for their April SiriusXM appearance because they weren't prepared. Otis Pavlovic said there was less thought behind it than it might sound.
The "Linger / Heading For The Door (Sirius XM Session)" release came out on 31 May 2024 and runs 3:06 for "Linger". The label credit is OURNESS PTY LTD.
The band released the live SiriusXM session on 31 May 2024. A June 2024 post from them called "Heading For The Door" one of their favourite songs to perform live.
The cover gave Royel Otis their first Billboard Hot 100 entry, debuting at No. 94 on the chart dated Aug. 10, 2024.
Paste reported that the "Linger" cover had outpaced their "Murder on the Dancefloor" success, with 18 million YouTube views and 72 million streams.
Royel Otis are a Sydney indie pop duo formed in 2019 by Royel Maddell and Otis Pavlovic. Their debut album Pratts & Pain was released on 16 February 2024 and produced by Dan Carey.

research.lineage: The cover sits in the Australian indie-pop and guitar-pop duo tradition, where viral reinterpretations of earlier hits (Sophie Ellis-Bextor's "Murder on the Dancefloor", then The Cranberries' 1990s alt-rock "Linger") became a key part of the duo's rise.

draft:
"Do you have to let it linger?" is not really a question. It's a plea from someone who can't leave and wants the other person to do the leaving for them. In **Linger**, Royel Otis keep that plea intact and set it over a clean, bright electric guitar picking out arpeggiated chords. A walking bass line and a steady kick, snare, and hi-hat drive it at a moderate tempo. The sound is easy to like, and the words underneath it are not easy at all.

The song belongs to The Cranberries, whose 1992 original was written by Dolores O'Riordan, with the music composed by O'Riordan and Noel Hogan. Its narrator holds evidence and still can't act on it. "So why were you holding her hand?" lands as a direct hit, and the questions that follow ("Were you lying all the time?") show someone circling an answer they already know. The craft is in the self-protection mixed into the hurt. "I'm sure I might be rude but it's just your attitude" apologizes and accuses in one breath, as if the narrator has to excuse their own anger before they're allowed to feel it. Then the chorus gives up the fight: "You've got me wrapped around your finger / Do you have to let it linger?" The pride and the surrender never settle. By the end the verses fall away and only the chorus is left, "do you have to" stacked three times, the plea repeating because nothing has changed.

Royel Otis, the Sydney duo of Royel Maddell and Otis Pavlovic, sing it in a clear, slightly nasal voice with a relaxed, nearly conversational delivery, and a second voice comes in to harmonize. That ease turns the song into something more resigned and less wounded. It's heartbreak told to a friend after the worst has passed. The harmony helps, making the confession sound shared rather than private. The production is polished and the groove holds one steady gear. If there's a drag, it's that the band never pushes against the lyric's desperation, but the restraint suits a narrator who has stopped expecting anything.

They recorded it for SiriusXM's Alt Nation in New York, picking the song in a panic because they weren't prepared. Pavlovic said there was less thought behind it than it might sound. It became their first Billboard Hot 100 entry, debuting at No. 94, and Paste reported it had outpaced their "Murder on the Dancefloor" cover with 72 million streams. Maybe that lack of planning is why it works. It sounds like a song they already knew by heart.

The bright, unbothered strum keeps you humming along until you notice you're singing the plea of someone who knows they're being lied to and still can't let go.
